"When things like that happen throughout the game or throughout the season, it’s like — it does make it hard, I feel like, for us to go back and play," St. Brown said. "It’s like, damn, we just — we took care of him, put him on a stretcher, sent him out back to the hospital, and now we gotta go play again. So, that kinda sucks, I feel like."

Although St. Brown said returning to the game was difficult, the 27-year-old acknowledged that injuries are part of playing such a violent sport.

"But, you know, it’s what I signed up for; it’s what we signed up for. We get paid a lot of money to play this sport that we love. And so, we’ve gotta finish the game and things like that. But I think injuries like that make it — it makes you put things into perspective, and I think he has done that for a lot of us on our team."

"I’m thinking about Jack; we’re all thinking about Jack. We hope he continues to get better, and yeah, all we can do is pray for him."

Campbell expressed his love for his teammates and the Detroit community after receiving an outpouring of support following his injury.

"To my teammates, coaches, and everyone in the Lions organization, I want you to know how much I love and appreciate you. This team is a family to me, and the way everyone has been there for me means everything. I’m proud to be a Detroit Lion and couldn’t ask to be surrounded by a better group of people. One thing I’ve learned about Detroit is that this city is built on toughness, resilience, and grit. That’s exactly how I’m going to approach this challenge," Campbell said in the statement.

"Please continue to keep me and my family in your prayers. We feel the love, and I can’t thank everyone enough. God is good. My faith is strong."

item.title: Erika Kirk channels Charlie with blunt message to conservatives after GOP midterm losses
item.description: Erika Kirk invoked her late husband Charlie Kirk's words, urging conservatives to stay positive and avoid infighting after election setbacks.
item.content:encoded:
Erika Kirk had a message for conservatives reeling from Republican election setbacks, and she turned to her late husband Charlie’s words to deliver it.

"I miss Charlie so much every single day, but especially on a day like today," she wrote.

"He always said that when things are going well, we need to stay humble. And when things aren’t going the way we want, we need to stay positive, keep our faith, and get back to work."

ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION

The widow of Turning Point USA CEO and founder Charlie Kirk said her husband had built a political operation meant to endure both victories and defeats.

"Charlie’s vision for Turning Point Action was always bigger than one election," she wrote. "He wanted a permanent, year-round operation with the people, relationships, and resources to compete in every cycle.

INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES

"He knew there would be victories and setbacks because he had experienced both and that’s why he built for both."

Kirk also thanked the staff, students, volunteers and ballot chasers who worked during the election cycle.

ERIKA KIRK SAYS PRESIDENTIAL LIBRARY-STYLE TRIBUTE TO CHARLIE KIRK IS 'IN THE WORKS' AS TPUSA EXPANDS

"I know Charlie would be unbelievably proud of each and every one of you, and I am, too," she wrote.

In a lengthy post on X, Erika Kirk said Republicans saw once comfortable races tighten or flip as candidates she described as democratic socialists campaigned on the cost of gas, groceries and housing.

FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'

"A rising stock market doesn’t mean much when nearly half of Americans don’t have a 401K and just want to put gas in their trucks, put food on the table, and provide a good life for their families," she wrote.

Erika Kirk paired her warning with a defense of free enterprise, arguing conservatives must understand why voters looked elsewhere without embracing the policies their opponents offered.

CALLING DEMOCRATS ‘COMMUNISTS’ WON’T WIN GEN Z — REPUBLICANS NEED A BETTER OFFER

"We can disagree with the solutions voters were offered while still recognizing why they were looking elsewhere for answers," she wrote.

Erika Kirk warned conservatives against turning on one another as she urged them to take voters’ frustrations seriously.

JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026

"The biggest mistake conservatives can make right now would be to allow this moment to become another exercise in finger-pointing, in-fighting, or trying to secure their own political preservation," she wrote. 

"That does not solve the problems the American people are demanding be solved."

Erika Kirk said exit polls showed voters were concerned about the economy and the war in Iran. 

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS

She said those concerns echoed what Turning Point had been hearing from students around the country for months.

"This isn’t a surprise to us because we’ve heard the same concerns from our students around the country for months and we’ve been concerned about it too," she wrote.

JONATHAN TURLEY: SOCIALISM IS BACK IN STYLE, AND DEMOCRATS ARE BUYING THE PITCH

Erika Kirk rejected socialism as an answer, arguing it places economic power in government hands rather than allowing individuals and families to build prosperity.

She said that approach conflicts with the free enterprise, individual liberty and opportunity at the heart of the country.

But she also warned that Americans will not simply stick with a party out of habit.

"Americans are not looking for labels and don’t subscribe to unquestioned party loyalty anymore either," she wrote. "They will support the candidates who can both speak to their concerns and deliver on what THEY need and dream about for their families."

She identified affordable homes, safe communities and greater opportunity for the next generation as the promises voters want fulfilled.

Erika Kirk said the organization would study the results, listen to voters and spend the next two years making the case that conservative policies and free markets can address the problems Americans face.

She pledged to continue building relationships in communities across the country and preparing for "2028 and beyond."

"Our principles haven’t changed and neither has our mission," she wrote.

"Onward."

item.title: DSA leader dismisses $49T cost estimate for socialist policies as a 'made-up number'
item.description: DSA co-chair Megan Romer dismissed the White House's $49 trillion price tag for socialist policies as a "made-up number" and declined to offer her own.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) national co-chair Megan Romer was pressed on Fox News about how much socialist policies will cost American taxpayers after DSA-backed candidates made significant gains in midterm elections.

The White House Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) estimated that DSA policy proposals, including Medicare for All and student debt cancellation, would cost taxpayers $49 trillion. Romer, who said the group's incoming lawmakers will prioritize affordability, dismissed the staggering price tag as "outrageous," calling it a "made-up number."

"The White House, who does not like us very much, managed to come up with some math that made us look bad," Romer said on "The Story." "But we don't agree with these numbers."

RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY

The CEA’s report estimated the DSA’s policy wish list will cost about $355,000 per American household over the next decade.

After rejecting the administration's figures, Romer declined to offer an independent estimate of her own when pressed by Fox News anchor Martha MacCallum, saying the cost "depends."

DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES ARE WINNING PRIMARIES AND THEIR VISION FOR AMERICA IS VERY DIFFERENT

"There's no, like, one, solid number because it depends on what pieces we can build in the meantime," the DSA leader said. "So it's about building up programs and then sunsetting old, bad programs, and that number is going to shift as we pass various things."

"I'm not going to give you a solid number. That's not what I'm here to do," she continued. "What I'm here to do is talk about how we collectively can democratically decide how we want our money to be spent."

SOCIALIST PRIMARY SWEEP SPARKS LAUNCH OF NEW RESOURCE LAYING OUT WHAT’S AT STAKE IN 2026

Romer criticized the scale of U.S. military spending, arguing that federal resources devoted to overseas military operations would be better redirected toward the DSA's policy priorities, including amnesty for illegal immigrants and abolishing the Senate.

"We don't believe in having 800 U.S. military bases around the world," Romer said. "That is an insane amount of money to spend… Our military spending is outrageous, and most of that money is going to defense contractors. It is making a handful of billionaires richer."

SEN DEB FISCHER: THE LEFT'S WAR ON THE SENATE AND SUPREME COURT PUTS OUR REPUBLIC AT RISK

MacCallum countered her claims about excessive military spending, saying the U.S. defense budget is only $961 billion compared to an estimated $47 trillion for DSA policies to be funded.

In a July interview with Fox News, Romer stood by her positions to abolish the Senate, replace the presidency and Supreme Court, and to eradicate Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She also defended wanting to abolish borders and grant amnesty to illegal immigrants in the United States.

"We do agree that it will cost money to provide healthcare to everyone, but it will cost less money than we spend on the military and on these illegal wars right now," Romer said Wednesday.

item.title: Idaho voters focused on the real issues during midterms, like choosing the Winchester 1873 as their state gun
item.description: Idaho voters chose the Winchester Model 1873 as the official state gun, making it one of 11 U.S. states with an official firearm designation.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday's midterm elections were a bit of a bloodbath for the Republican Party.

If you're a conservative, chances are you are looking for any silver lining to cope with the fact that Democrats took the GOP behind the woodshed last night.

I'm here to tell you it wasn't all bad, though, as states like Tennessee and Florida are still looking pretty red, so there's no need to get too down in the dumps.

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

One state that certainly has voters with their priorities straight is Idaho, and I'm not just saying that because their state GOP incumbents completed a clean sweep at the polls.

It seems the voters all throughout The Gem State were focused on the real issues that have been at the top of everyone's mind.

Not healthcare or grocery prices, but rather which firearm would become the official state gun of Idaho.

No, I'm not kidding.

Six different firearms were presented on the ballot, presenting quite a grab bag of options, from a Colt .45 to an M1 Garand.

And the winner is...

And what a winner we have!

The Winchester Model 1873, aka "The Gun that Won the West," is now the official state gun of Idaho.

Man, what a crushing blow for the "Peacemaker," I was sure he was going to pull away late.

In all seriousness, that's a pretty cool thing to say.

Some states have an official marine mammal or dessert, but Idaho has a state gun.

CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES

It’s actually not uncommon, either, as 11 U.S. states now have an official firearm.

Most of the states on the list are pretty predictable, including Texas and West Virginia. I was surprised to see Pennsylvania included, though, while my beloved Sunshine State is nowhere to be found.

Regardless, whenever your conservative buddies get a little down in the dumps this week, just remind them that Idaho now has a state gun.

That'll go a long way in "owning the libs!"

item.title: CBB With Danny Z: Kansas, Tennessee and USC lead another human polls vs. analytics argument
item.description: Kansas ranks outside the AP top 15 but fifth in KenPom, highlighting major splits among four college basketball ranking systems this preseason.
item.content:encoded:
College basketball is back, and so is "CBB With Danny Z." Try to contain your excitement (I'm genuinely psyched that college hoops is back, but I understand that many people don't even realize college basketball exists until February or March).

Last season, we kicked off a series comparing the preseason AP Top 25 with KenPom's rankings, then checked back in December, January and March to see how those disagreements developed.

UCONN BASKETBALL COACH FLOATS POTENTIAL GAME AT WHITE HOUSE AFTER UFC EVENT

KenPom deserves some credit for Vanderbilt last season. It ranked the Commodores 19th in the preseason, while the AP voters had them effectively 36th. Vanderbilt finished 27-9, earned a No. 5 seed and won an NCAA Tournament game. But KenPom also had Baylor 17th in the preseason. The Bears finished 17-17 and missed the tournament.

St. John’s was a reminder to be careful about declaring a winner in December. The AP’s preseason No. 5 team started 4-3, which initially made KenPom’s more cautious ranking of 16th look pretty smart. Then the Red Storm finished 30-7, reached the Sweet 16 as a No. 5 seed and pushed Duke in an 80-75 loss. The voters’ optimism looked considerably more reasonable by the end of the season.

The AP voters had their own problems with Creighton. They put the Bluejays 23rd in the preseason, while KenPom had them all the way down at 41st. Creighton finished 16–18 and missed the NCAA Tournament, settling for a trip to the College Basketball Crown. I’m guessing that wasn’t the postseason tournament those voters had in mind.

So, there’s a reason to keep track of these disagreements. This year, we’re giving ourselves a few more to follow. Alongside KenPom, I’m adding TeamRankings’ predictive ratings to the comparison, plus the Coaches Poll. Before we get too carried away arguing about humans versus computers, we should probably find out whether the humans agree with each other. Or the computers, for that matter.

The comparisons below use the preseason AP and Coaches polls and both analytics models' ratings from the morning of November 1, before the season began.

The top of the board offers relatively little controversy. Both human polls put Florida first and Duke second. Both analytics models reverse that order. Illinois is third in both polls and fourth in both models. Everybody likes those three teams.

After that, things get more interesting. The blue-blood Kansas Jayhawks represent one of the biggest disagreements entering this season, and the surprising part is who likes them more.

It’s the computers.

Kansas is No. 17 in the AP Poll and tied for 18th in the Coaches Poll. KenPom has the Jayhawks fifth and TeamRankings puts them sixth.

I would have expected the voters to be higher on a historically great program like Kansas. Seeing both computers put the Jayhawks in the top six while neither human poll has them in the top 15 definitely caught me by surprise.

Iowa State is another team where we see major disagreement. The Cyclones were a No. 2 seed in the 2026 NCAA Tournament but enter this season ranked 18th by the AP and tied for 14th with the coaches. KenPom has them sixth.

TeamRankings puts Iowa State 11th, higher than either human poll but below KenPom. The Cyclones’ defense helps explain KenPom’s optimism: he projects it to be the second-best unit in the country.

Alabama is another program getting more love from the models. The Crimson Tide are 20th in the AP Poll and tied for 18th in the Coaches Poll, compared with ninth in KenPom and 16th at TeamRankings. KenPom projects Alabama to have the nation’s fourth-best offense.

Houston rounds out that group. The Cougars are third in KenPom and seventh at TeamRankings, ahead of their placements in the AP Poll (10th) and Coaches Poll (eighth). KenPom gives Houston the top defensive projection in the country.

USC might be the best example of why this exercise is worth doing. Both groups of voters awarded the Trojans a preseason Top 25 ranking (21st by the AP and 22nd by the coaches), while neither model placed the Trojans inside the top 35. KenPom has them 37th, and TeamRankings puts them 40th.

Tennessee presents an even more interesting argument near the top of the polls. The Volunteers are eighth in the AP and ninth in the Coaches Poll. The analytics are considerably less impressed: 22nd in KenPom and 18th at TeamRankings.

If you followed last year's series, that might sound a little backward. Tennessee was a KenPom favorite last preseason, sitting ninth in the model compared with 18th in the AP Poll. This time, the voters are the optimistic ones. For what it’s worth, the Volunteers reached the Elite Eight as a No. 6 seed before losing to top-seeded Michigan.

Arkansas belongs on the watch list, too. The Razorbacks are 12th in the AP Poll and 13th with the coaches, but KenPom places them 19th and TeamRankings has them 25th. The Razorbacks reached the Sweet 16 in 2026.

JOHN CALIPARI JOKES THAT HE WAS 'ON CRACK' WHEN PUTTING TOGETHER ARKANSAS' WILDLY DIFFICULT SCHEDULE

BYU lands 25th in both human polls, while both models leave the Cougars outside the Top 25: 34th in KenPom and 30th at TeamRankings.

St. John’s offers another familiar disagreement: AP No. 13 and tied for 14th with the coaches, compared with 21st in KenPom and 17th at TeamRankings. Last preseason, the AP had the Red Storm fifth while KenPom ranked them 16th. The gap is smaller this time, but the voters are higher on St. John’s again.

Nebraska was one of the best stories in last year's series because neither side saw the Huskers coming. They began outside KenPom's top 50 without receiving a single preseason AP vote, then climbed into the top 15 of both rankings by our March update.

This year's starting positions are very different. KenPom has Nebraska 15th and TeamRankings puts the Huskers 22nd. The human voters at least noticed Nebraska this year. The Cornhuskers are just outside both Top 25s, effectively 27th in the AP Poll and 26th in the Coaches Poll. Nebraska is coming off a 28-7 season that included the first Sweet 16 appearance in program history.

Ohio State is another unranked team KenPom likes, placing the Buckeyes 18th. TeamRankings has them 31st, though, which brings us to the complication with treating "the analytics" as a single opinion.

Vanderbilt should be familiar to anyone who read these columns last season. KenPom consistently liked the Commodores more than the AP voters did, and the same disagreement is back. Vanderbilt is 12th in KenPom, compared with 24th in the AP Poll and 21st with the coaches.

After following these rankings last season, I think the humans put more weight on how teams finished the previous year. Vanderbilt didn’t make it out of the first weekend of the NCAA Tournament, and I suspect that’s part of why the voters aren’t as high on the Commodores as KenPom is.

TeamRankings has Vanderbilt 24th, exactly where the AP puts the Commodores, so KenPom is sort of on an island here with its optimism for the Commodores in 2026-27.

UConn gives us a different split. The Huskies are fourth in the AP Poll and fifth in the Coaches Poll. That's not surprising considering UConn is coming off a national championship game appearance and won back-to-back titles in 2023 and 2024.

KenPom isn't as high on Dan Hurley's squad, though, and ranks them 11th. This seems like a slam-dunk case of the humans being on board with a perennial powerhouse while the analytics see a team set to take a step back.

Except TeamRankings has UConn third, making the model more optimistic than either human poll.

Louisville offers a smaller version of the same argument. Both human polls have the Cardinals 11th, between KenPom at 16th and TeamRankings at ninth.

We'll revisit these starting points as the season develops and see whether the humans or the computers are better at projecting how the season will play out. We'll also see whether one model outperforms the other and whether the coaches do a better job than the media.

Want something included in the next "CBB With Danny Z"? Email me at dan.zaksheske@outkick.com or find me on X: @RealDanZak.

item.title: JACKSON THOMPSON: Democrat-appointed judges hand Letitia James win over county trying to protect girls sports
item.description: A four-judge panel found Nassau County's transgender athlete ban conflicts with New York's Human Rights Law, but the county vows to appeal it.
item.content:encoded:
A New York appeals court Wednesday struck down Nassau County’s law barring transgender girls and women from women’s sports teams using county facilities, handing Attorney General Letitia James a victory in her legal battle with Bruce Blakeman.

The unanimous ruling by a four-judge panel of the Appellate Division, Second Department, reversed a lower-court decision upholding the restrictions. The judges found that the county law conflicted with New York’s statewide antidiscrimination protections.

Nassau County Attorney Thomas Adams indicated the county would continue fighting.

"We are reviewing the decision with the intention to continue the appeals process," Adams said in a statement.

The decision came one day after Blakeman lost his gubernatorial challenge to Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul. James also won reelection Tuesday.

All four judges who joined the ruling were elevated to the appellate court by Democratic governors. Former Gov. Andrew Cuomo appointed Justice Betsy Barros in April 2014 and Justice Deborah Dowling in June 2021. Hochul appointed Justice Barry Warhit in May 2022 and announced Justice Lisa Ottley’s selection earlier this year.

State election records list Barros, Dowling and Warhit as Democratic candidates in their judicial election histories. Ottley ran for state Supreme Court in 2018 on the Democratic, Republican and Conservative ballot lines, according to New York City’s official voter guide.

'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' LEGAL DEFENSE AND TRANS ATHLETE'S ATTORNEYS SPEAK OUT AFTER LANDMARK SCOTUS RULING

The appeals court held that Nassau’s permit restrictions were preempted by the state Human Rights Law and Civil Rights Law, which prohibit discrimination based on gender identity or expression. It directed the lower court to enter a judgment declaring the measure invalid under the state Constitution and Municipal Home Rule Law.

"Nobody should have to fight to play the game they love. Transgender athletes have the right to play on the court, field, or roller rink like everyone else, and today the Second Department made clear that Nassau County cannot ban them," James said in a statement.

"No one asked for this illegal and exclusionary policy. Bruce Blakeman was just trying to stop athletes from playing with their teammates. I am pleased the court saw right through it."

The county law required organizations seeking permits for sporting events at county facilities to designate themselves as male, female or coed based on biological sex at birth. It prohibited permits for female events that allowed male competitors, while permitting female athletes in male and coed categories.

The restrictions did not prohibit transgender athletes from all sports participation. They prevented teams designated for women or girls from obtaining county permits if they included transgender female competitors.

The measure affected more than 100 county facilities, including athletic fields, basketball and tennis courts, swimming pools and ice rinks, according to James’ office.

INSIDE THE SUPREME COURT BATTLE TO 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS'

Blakeman first imposed the policy through a February 2024 executive order. After a judge struck down that order on the grounds that he lacked authority to issue it, the county Legislature passed legislation reinstating the restrictions. Blakeman signed the law July 15, 2024, prompting separate lawsuits from James and the New York Civil Liberties Union.

The NYCLU represented the Long Island Roller Rebels, an adult women’s roller derby league that welcomes transgender participants.

State Supreme Court Justice R. Bruce Cozzens upheld the law in October 2025, accepting the county’s safety and fairness arguments and reasoning that transgender athletes could participate in coed leagues. The county also argued that Title IX supported its use of biological sex to separate athletic categories.

However, the Second Department separately granted the Roller Rebels a preliminary injunction in October 2025, reversing Cozzens’ earlier refusal to temporarily block enforcement.

NEWSOM FACES CRITICISM FOR STATE'S STANCE ON TRANS ATHLETES IN GIRLS' SPORTS AFTER SCOTUS RULING

In that decision, the appeals court found that limited access to private facilities had reduced the league’s practice opportunities and hurt its ranking. It also found that requiring the league to identify as mixed-sex could jeopardize its governing-body status and ability to find opponents.

The litigation unfolded alongside a broader national fight over transgender eligibility in female sports.

In June, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the challenged restrictions in West Virginia and Idaho, concluding that schools could determine eligibility for female teams by biological sex under Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause.

That ruling permitted the challenged state policies; it did not require every state to adopt such restrictions. Nassau’s case instead turned on whether the county could impose a permit policy that conflicted with New York state law.

"As long as I am attorney general, no New Yorker will be shut out of public life because of who they are," James said.

item.title: San Francisco 49ers coach shuts down reunion talks as Brandon Aiyuk seeks NFL reinstatement
item.description: Kyle Shanahan says he has "no expectation" of Brandon Aiyuk returning to the 49ers despite the receiver's reinstatement filing with Drew Rosenhaus.
item.content:encoded:
Brandon Aiyuk won't be getting a warm welcome back in San Francisco after walking away from the team and embarking on an erratic, self-destructive stretch that has effectively alienated him from the NFL.

49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan officially slammed the door on a reunion Wednesday. Despite San Francisco’s depleted receiver room, the organization has no intention of bringing Aiyuk back, even after the former All-Pro claimed he is cleaning up his act.

When asked Wednesday about Aiyuk's apparent turnaround, Shanahan was blunt.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"None. I have no expectation," Shanahan said. "I’ve kind of moved on with that mentally and doing kind of how I talked to you guys two months ago. Nothing’s really changed for me."

Aiyuk filed for NFL reinstatement this week alongside new agent Drew Rosenhaus and is scheduled to report Friday, though the 49ers do not plan to retain him. While general manager John Lynch previously struck a softer tone regarding a potential return for the expensive wideout, Shanahan’s position has remained firm.

Aiyuk spent months burning bridges across the organization. He severed ties with the franchise through an acrimonious contract standoff, an off-field reckless speeding citation and completely ghosting team medical staff during injury rehabilitation.

After San Francisco voided his future contract guarantees and sidelined him, Aiyuk went scorched-earth on social media. He blasted the organization as "stupid," accused Lynch of showing up uninvited at his home and hurled insults at front-office personnel and assistant coaches.

Beyond mocking Shanahan’s demeanor and leadership, Aiyuk drew severe backlash for taking thinly veiled jabs at Shanahan’s car accident in July, posting Instagram stories telling him to "stay in yo own lane" and declaring that "you can't win the race if you crash out."

Before the fallout, Aiyuk stood as one of San Francisco’s most dynamic offensive playmakers. Selected 25th overall in the 2020 NFL Draft, he developed into the team’s primary perimeter target, posting consecutive 1,000-yard receiving campaigns in 2022 and 2023. His peak came in 2023, when he earned Second-Team All-Pro honors after amassing 1,342 receiving yards and playing a pivotal role in San Francisco’s run to Super Bowl LVIII. Across five seasons in the Bay Area, Aiyuk totaled 294 receptions for 4,305 yards and 25 touchdowns.

Under contract through 2028 with $27 million in guarantees already voided, releasing Aiyuk leaves San Francisco with a $12.35 million dead-cap hit, finally clearing the path for him to pursue opportunities elsewhere.
